stories.headline: Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte Impeached for Second Time
stories.summary:
The Philippine House of Representatives voted Monday to impeach Vice President Sara Duterte for the second time, with 255 of 290 lawmakers in attendance supporting the measure — far exceeding the one-third threshold required. The case now moves to the Senate for trial, where a conviction would disqualify Duterte from holding public office, effectively ending her bid for the presidency in 2028.

The charges stem from alleged misuse of public funds and death threats Duterte reportedly made against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., his wife, and his cousin, then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez. Duterte and Marcos were once allies who won the 2022 election by a landslide, but their partnership collapsed as they pursued conflicting political agendas. The first impeachment attempt in 2025 was blocked by the Supreme Court on a technicality before a Senate trial could begin.

Duterte's legal team dismissed the charges as 'nothing more than a scrap of paper' and called the proceedings politically motivated. She refused to appear at committee hearings and did not publicly address the allegations. The scale of Monday's House vote is widely seen as a measure of Marcos' consolidated power in the lower chamber.

Conviction in the Senate remains uncertain. Unlike House members, who are elected by district and tend to align with the sitting president, senators are elected nationally and are considered more independent. Candidates allied with Duterte outperformed Marcos-backed rivals in last year's midterm elections, and Duterte currently leads presidential preference surveys by 17 points over her nearest rival.

stories.headline: Democrats Hold Modest Lead in 2026 Congressional Generic Ballot Polling
stories.summary:
Early polling ahead of the 2026 midterm elections shows Democrats with a consistent but narrow advantage on the congressional generic ballot, according to an aggregation published by The New York Times. The data, drawn from a broad range of recent surveys, shows Democrats leading in the large majority of polls, though typically by single-digit margins. The pattern is consistent with the historical tendency for the party out of the White House to gain ground during midterm cycles.

However, analysts caution that national polling averages may not translate directly into seat gains. Redistricting efforts currently underway in multiple states following recent court rulings could significantly alter the number of votes Democrats would need to reclaim a House majority. The interaction between popular vote share and district maps remains a critical variable.

Republicans argue that structural advantages built through redistricting, combined with the enthusiasm of the president's base, could blunt or reverse any generic ballot disadvantage. Democrats counter that high disapproval ratings for the administration, particularly on economic issues, are driving their polling gains and will hold through November.

All 435 House seats and one-third of Senate seats will be contested in November 2026. Control of both chambers remains genuinely competitive, with the outcome likely to hinge on economic conditions, candidate quality in swing districts, and the final shape of newly drawn congressional maps.

stories.headline: Eurovision Faces Largest Boycott in 70-Year History Over Israel's Inclusion
stories.summary:
The 2026 Eurovision Song Contest, held this week in Austria, is confronting the largest broadcaster boycott in the competition's seven-decade history. Broadcasters from Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Iceland, and Slovenia have withdrawn from the event in protest of Israel's continued participation, amid the ongoing war in Gaza. Thirty-five countries are still participating despite the walkouts.

The controversy intensified following last year's contest in Basel, where Israeli singer Yuval Raphael received the highest public vote total of any contestant but was beaten overall by Austria. Two protesters attempted to rush the stage during the grand final, and anti-Israel demonstrations drew hundreds outside the venue. Several participating broadcasters questioned the validity of the public vote, noting that Israeli government social media accounts — including Prime Minister Netanyahu's — urged supporters to vote the maximum 20 times for Israel's entry.

The European Broadcasting Union confirmed an independent audit found no evidence that voting up to 20 times disproportionately affected the final result, and called the outcome valid and robust. The Israeli government has maintained it faces a coordinated global smear campaign. Critics of Israel's inclusion argue that a state engaged in an active military conflict should not compete in a contest premised on cultural cooperation and shared values.

The dispute has reignited longstanding debates about whether geopolitical conflicts should affect Eurovision eligibility and whether the public voting system is susceptible to coordinated campaigning. Organizers are under growing pressure to review both Israel's status and the mechanics of viewer voting ahead of the 2026 final.

stories.headline: Thailand's Former PM Thaksin Shinawatra Released from Prison
stories.summary:
Former Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra was released Monday from Bangkok's Klong Prem prison after serving part of a one-year sentence for corruption and abuses of power dating to his 2001–2006 tenure. Hundreds of red-shirted supporters gathered outside the prison to greet the 76-year-old, who told reporters he was in good health and 'relieved.' He was met by family members including his daughter and political protégé, former Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra.

Thaksin's release comes after a turbulent period for his political network. He was jailed in September 2025 after the Supreme Court ruled that his earlier hospitalization had been used to avoid serving his sentence — a ruling that followed the Constitutional Court's dismissal of his daughter as prime minister over a leaked phone call concerning a border dispute with Cambodia. Those back-to-back judicial rulings underscored the persistent influence of Thailand's conservative courts over Thaksin-aligned governments.

Thaksin's Pheu Thai party insists he will remain in the background of politics going forward, but analysts and supporters alike expressed skepticism. One supporter who drove more than 700 kilometers to witness his release told the BBC she hoped Thaksin would continue to help the country, saying 'only he can deliver what he promised.'

Thaksin has dominated Thai politics for more than two decades, surviving multiple coups, years of exile, and repeated court rulings against his allies. His return to public life — even in a nominally private capacity — is expected to energize his base ahead of future electoral contests and complicate the political calculations of rival factions.
